items.title: Flappy Fish: Genetic Algorithm Game
items.summary: Group Pygame project that turns a Flappy Bird-style game into a genetic-algorithm experiment, comparing manual play with AI fish that evolve over generations.
items.content_html:
Flappy Fish was a group project that turned a simple arcade idea into an evolutionary-learning experiment. The base game works like an underwater Flappy Bird: a fish moves through scrolling obstacles, survives by passing through gaps, and loses when it collides with plants, borders, or pipes. The project is not only about making the game playable; it is about using the same game environment to compare manual control with automated agents that learn over time.

What the project does

The game has two main modes. In manual mode, a player controls one fish directly, which made it easier to test the physics, obstacle timing, scoring, collisions, and overall feel of the game. In simulation mode, the keyboard input is replaced by a population of AI-controlled fish. Each fish plays the same level, receives a fitness score based on survival and progress, and contributes to the next generation if it performs well.

How the AI learns

The learning system is based on a genetic algorithm. Each fish has a small set of weights that acts like its genome. On every frame, the agent reads simple state values such as the vertical distance to the next gap, the horizontal distance to the obstacle, and its current vertical speed. Those values are combined by the policy to decide whether the fish should flap. After a generation ends, the strongest fish are selected, crossed over, and mutated so the next generation can inherit better behavior while still exploring new strategies.

Architecture

The code is organized so the game loop, fish physics, obstacle generation, UI screens, and genetic-algorithm logic stay separated. That separation matters because the same environment has to support two different control systems: a human player in manual mode and many autonomous agents in simulation mode. The web demo also adds a deployment layer around the original Pygame work, including score and leaderboard behavior.

Group work and contributors

This was group work. The public GitHub contributors are mariia-osipova, mroldan-netizen, julietazanoni, santugituni, and SantuCode11.

What I worked on

My part focused on implementation, algorithm and game integration, documentation, and deployment polish. In the repo, my commits include finishing the Fish and Game modules, tuning fish physics and collision behavior, building the genetic-algorithm simulation with generations, weights, genes, and a 100-fish population, adding simulation UI details, improving screenshots and README material, adapting the web demo, and connecting score and leaderboard sync through Google Sheets and a server proxy.

Why it was useful

This project made the genetic algorithm feel concrete. Small changes to fitness scoring, mutation, selection pressure, physics, or collision rules immediately changed what happened on screen. That made it a good systems project: the algorithm only works when the game loop, state representation, scoring, UI, and deployment details all line up.

Links: deployed Flappy Fish app and Flappy Fish on GitHub.

items.title: Cheese Agent: A FastAPI RAG Chatbot with Vector Search
items.summary: AI-powered cheese agent built with FastAPI, AstraDB vector search, OpenAI, and a lightweight JS frontend.
items.content_html:
This post is about my experience building Cheese Agent, a cheese-themed RAG chatbot project with a FastAPI backend, OpenAI embeddings, AstraDB vector search, and a vanilla JS frontend.

What this post is

This is a short technical reflection on building Cheese Agent, especially the parts that made it feel like a real systems project rather than just a UI experiment.

Why I made it

I wanted to build something that combined an interface people would actually enjoy using with a backend architecture that forced me to think about retrieval quality, data organization, and deployment.

How it works

The backend exposes a chat endpoint in FastAPI. When a user sends a question, the backend embeds that query with OpenAI, searches AstraDB, and sends the retrieved context into the generation step.

What I focused on in the implementation

The most useful parts for me were the ingestion script, the vector database, and the split between a simple frontend and a backend that handled retrieval and answer generation.

What seems promising so far

This kind of project is useful because it combines data preparation, embeddings, retrieval, API design, frontend integration, and deployment in one place.

Closing thoughts

For me, Cheese Agent became a compact full-stack AI project where the model, the database, the data pipeline, and the interface all had to line up.
